transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, it's a bit of a long story, but I guess the main thing that brings me in is... well, my father-in-law recently moved in with us. And, you know, my wife and I, we always said we'd take care of family when the time came, but having him in the house full-time has just completely shifted the entire dynamic of our home. 

I mean, I can hold it together perfectly fine at work. I’m an EMT, so I'm pretty used to compartmentalizing high-stress situations. When the sirens are on and I'm in the back of the rig, I'm totally dialed in, just doing my job like always. But the second my shift ends and I walk through my front door... I just, I don't know, I'm so incredibly wound up. I'm snapping at people, being way more short-tempered than I ever usually am. It's like I have this constant tension humming in the background. And it's bleeding into my coursework, too—I'm taking some classes to finish up my bachelor's degree, and I just can't seem to settle down and focus on the assignments without getting frustrated. 

And I think what really made me realize I needed to come in and talk to somebody is that the things I usually do to decompress, the stuff that usually keeps my head clear? I've just completely stopped doing them. I haven't been out fishing in weeks, which is usually my weekend sanctuary. I haven't touched any of my woodworking projects out in the garage—the tools are just gathering dust—and I’ve even started skipping these community first-aid workshops that I usually really enjoy helping out with. I just... I don't have the bandwidth for any of it right now, and I'm just so on edge all the time at home, it's really starting to wear me down.
Are you avoiding certain situations or activities because of your father-in-law moving in?

Well, no, I wouldn't really say I'm avoiding anything, not specifically because of him, anyway. It's not like I'm picking up extra shifts at the station just to keep away from the house, or, you know, hiding out somewhere to escape. I mean, my wife and I, we have a pretty decent-sized place—it's a split-level—so there's enough physical room for everyone to have their own corner. It's not a spatial issue where I feel like I have to flee the premises. 

And as for the activities I mentioned, like the fishing and the woodworking... it's not that I'm avoiding them because he's around or because he's trying to get involved in my hobbies or anything like that. Actually, he mostly stays in his room or sits in the living room watching his shows—he loves those old black-and-white Westerns, which is fine, but it's just this constant, lingering presence in the house now. 

So, no, I'm not actively avoiding situations or staying away to get away from him. It's really just that when I get home, all my energy just completely evaporates. I walk in, I see his stuff in the hallway, I hear the TV blaring, and I just feel this heavy, exhausting weight drop on my shoulders. I haven't stopped doing my projects to avoid him... I just literally don't have the drive to do them anymore because my battery is completely at zero by the time I cross the threshold. It's not avoidance, it's just... total depletion, if that makes sense.
Do you feel anxious when you're at home with your father-in-law?

Anxious? Hmm. I don't know if I'd really use the word anxious, to be honest. When I think of anxiety, I think of, you know, a racing heart or feeling panicked, like what I see in my patients when we get called out to a bad accident or somebody having a genuine panic attack. I see a lot of real, acute anxiety out on the rig. But at home with him... it's not like I'm sitting there worrying about the future or feeling scared of him or anything like that. 

It's more like... well, like I was trying to describe before, it's just this heavy, thick tension. Like, for example, just the other day I came home after a 12-hour shift—we had some pretty rough calls, just non-stop all day—and I walk through the door, and there he is at the kitchen table. He’s got his mail and his newspapers spread out all over the place, he’s doing this thing where he clicks his tongue while he reads, and that TV is just blaring from the living room. And looking at him, I didn't feel anxious. My chest didn't get tight with worry. I just felt this immediate, overwhelming spike of frustration, and just this complete draining of whatever patience I had left in the tank. 

My wife actually asked me something similar recently, she was like, are you anxious about my dad being here? And I had to explain to her, too, that it's not anxiety. I'm 51 years old, I've been doing this job long enough to know what anxiety looks like. This is just... it's like my sanctuary isn't mine anymore. It's just another place where I can't fully let my guard down and just be. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm anxious at all. Just wound up and completely worn out by the whole situation, if that makes sense.
Have you been experiencing any changes in your mood, such as feeling sad or depressed, since your father-in-law moved in?

Sad? No, I wouldn't say sad. And depressed... definitely not. I mean, I see people who are truly depressed out in the field, you know? We get calls for welfare checks all the time, people who haven't gotten out of bed in days, the shades drawn, just completely defeated by life. That's not me at all. I still get up every morning at 4:30 AM without fail, I make my coffee—black, just like I've had it for twenty years—and I head out to the station. And when I'm there, I'm joking around with my partner, we're shooting the breeze between calls, eating terrible diner food... I'm still me. I can still laugh and find the humor in things, even the dark humor you kind of need to survive in EMS. 

So, no, my mood hasn't dipped into sadness or feeling down in the dumps. It's really just... well, it's like a switch flips the second my boots hit the front porch. I don't feel like crying or anything like that. I don't feel hopeless about life in general. It's just that the house feels so incredibly crowded now. Like, just to give you an idea, I was looking at the living room the other day, and he's got this massive, overstuffed brown recliner he insisted on bringing from his old place, and it completely blocks the natural walkway to the sliding glass door out to the patio. Every single time I have to squeeze past it, I don't feel sad, I just feel this sharp spike of irritation. 

It's annoyance. It's feeling like I'm practically a guest in my own house now. I'll go into the kitchen to make a sandwich and his pill organizers are taking up half the counter, or the thermostat is cranked up to 78 degrees because his circulation isn't great, and I'm just sweating through my t-shirt trying to eat my lunch. None of that makes me want to weep, it just makes me want to grit my teeth. So yeah, depressed isn't the right word at all. I'm just irritable and totally drained by the logistics of it all. I just want my peace and quiet back, you know?
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

Lost interest? No, no, definitely not. I mean, if anything, I think I want to do those things more than ever, you know? Like I mentioned the woodworking earlier... I actually have this absolutely gorgeous piece of reclaimed oak sitting out on my workbench in the garage right now. I bought it maybe... well, it was right before my father-in-law moved in, actually. I was planning to build a new coffee table for the living room, ironically enough, since the old one got pushed into the corner to make room for his medical equipment. 

And I still really, really want to build it. I catch myself sketching out the joinery on scrap paper when my partner and I are sitting in the rig waiting for a dispatch call. I still love the idea of it, I still have all the passion for it. I love the smell of the sawdust, I love the focus it requires. And the fishing, same thing. I was just browsing through a catalog the other day during my lunch break, looking at some new lures, thinking about when the bass are going to start biting again. I haven't lost a single drop of interest in any of the things that make me, me. 

It's just... well, like I was trying to explain before, it's the energy. It's the execution of it. I have the desire, but then I walk through that front door after a long shift, I get hit with that wall of 78-degree heat, I hear the theme song to Gunsmoke playing at maximum volume, and whatever drive I had just evaporates. But the interest? The interest is absolutely 100 percent still there. I'd love nothing more than to spend six hours out on the lake or making sawdust in the garage. I just can't seem to muster the physical or mental energy to actually go do it once I'm trapped in that house. So, yeah, no loss of interest at all. Just... a total loss of momentum, I guess you could call it.
Are you staying away from certain parts of your home because of your father-in-law?

Staying away? Well... no. No, I definitely wouldn't say I'm staying away from anywhere. I mean, I can see why you'd ask that, given how much the whole situation gets under my skin, but at the end of the day, it's my house, you know? My wife and I bought that place, we've put a lot of blood, sweat, and tears into it. When you spend 12 hours a day working in the back of an ambulance—which is essentially a tiny, cramped, moving metal box that smells like bleach and whatever else we've had to clean up that shift—you really, really value your square footage at home. You want to be able to stretch out. So, no, I'm not about to let myself be chased out of my own living room or kitchen. 

Now, don't get me wrong, there are times when I pull into the driveway after a particularly brutal rotation, and I might just sit in the cab of my truck for an extra ten or fifteen minutes. Just sitting there in the driveway, listening to the engine tick as it cools down, staring at the porch light and trying to mentally brace myself for the 78-degree heat and the blaring TV. But once my boots are actually through that front door? I go wherever I need to go. 

If I want a glass of ice water, I march right into the kitchen, even if his pill bottles are everywhere and he's doing that tongue-clicking thing over his crossword puzzle. If I need to get to the patio, I squeeze right past that giant, overstuffed brown recliner of his. I might retreat to the garage to stare at my workbench, like I mentioned earlier, just to get five minutes of actual quiet, but I'm certainly not hiding out in the master bedroom or tiptoeing around the hallways to avoid him. I refuse to be a ghost in my own home. So, yeah, I'm not avoiding any parts of the house. I just walk through them with my jaw clenched tight enough to crack a tooth, but I'm still using the whole house.
Do you ever feel like you're disconnecting from yourself or your surroundings when you're at home with your father-in-law?

Disconnecting? Like... spacing out, or feeling like I'm not really there? Man, I honestly wish I could do that. That would probably be a blessing right now. But no, it's actually the exact opposite. I am painfully, agonizingly aware of everything going on around me in that house. 

I mean, in my line of work, you see people disconnect, right? You pull up to a bad MVA, a multi-car pileup, and you see a driver just sitting on the curb, staring right through you, completely detached from reality because their brain just... pulled the plug to protect them from the trauma and the shock. I know what that looks like. I deal with it all the time. And that is definitely not happening to me. 

If anything, I am hyper-connected to my surroundings when I'm home, to the point where it drives me absolutely crazy. I can't tune a single thing out. I sit there on the couch, and I feel every single degree of that 78-degree heat radiating through the room, just making the back of my neck sweat. I hear every single syllable of the local news anchor on the TV because he insists on having the volume cranked up to 45. I can hear him doing that tongue-clicking thing over his crossword puzzle from three rooms away, I can smell that weird menthol muscle rub he puts on his knees every evening at 7:00 PM sharp... it's like all my senses are dialed up to eleven. 

I can't escape it, not even for a minute. I don't feel detached from myself or the room at all. I just feel like myself, completely grounded, but trapped in this sort of sensory nightmare where I can't just relax and let my guard down. So, no, I'm not disconnecting or floating away or whatever you want to call it. I'm entirely, one hundred percent there. I just... I really, really don't want to be.
Do you ever feel like things around you aren't real when you're at home with your father-in-law?

Not real? Like I'm hallucinating or something? No, no, definitely not. It's all very, very real. Like I was just saying, I wish some of it wasn't real. I wish the volume on the TV wasn't real, or the heat, or the smell of that menthol rub. But no, everything is completely solid and real. 

I mean, I'm an EMT, I've seen people who are having psychotic breaks or who are under the influence of some serious substances, and they're swatting at things that aren't there or talking to people who don't exist. I know what that looks like, and I can assure you, that is absolutely not what's happening to me. I'm completely grounded in reality. The walls are solid, the TV is loud, and my father-in-law is sitting right there in his oversized recliner. 

Sometimes I'll be sitting there, trying to read a book or just decompress after a shift, and I'll look around the room, and I'll see the pile of medical bills on the counter, the oxygen tanks in the corner, the pill organizers... and I just think, "Wow, this is my life now." It's almost surreal in a way, just how much everything has changed so quickly, but it's not like I actually think it's an illusion or a dream or anything like that. It's just a very harsh, very loud, very warm reality that I'm trying to figure out how to navigate. So, no, everything feels completely real. Too real, if I'm being perfectly honest.
Are you doing things to try to avoid arguing or conflicting with your father-in-law?

Avoid arguing? You mean like... walking on eggshells around him? No. No, I wouldn't say I do that. Honestly, I just don't have the energy to put on a performance or try to manage someone else's mood at this point in my life. 

In my line of work, you have to be pretty direct. If you're on a chaotic scene, maybe a bad domestic call or someone panicking over a medical emergency, you don't have the luxury of time to worry about hurting someone's feelings or avoiding a conflict. You just have to take control and say, "Hey, I need you to step back," or "Sir, you need to hold still right now." That kind of bluntness, it just becomes a part of who you are after doing this job for as long as I have. It definitely bleeds into your personal life. 

So when I'm at home, and he's got the TV blasting the local news at volume 45 like I mentioned, and I'm just trying to eat a bowl of cereal in peace after a brutal night shift... I don't sit there agonizing over how to ask him to turn it down without upsetting him. I don't try to drop subtle hints or wait for him to leave the room. I just look at him and say, "Hey, turn the TV down a notch, I can't even hear myself think." And if he gets grumpy about it, well, he gets grumpy. He'll do that little huffing thing he does, maybe mutter something under his breath or click his tongue at me, but I really don't care. 

I'm not going to bend over backwards or change how I act just to keep the peace. My wife, bless her, she's the peacemaker of the house. She'll come in and say, "Oh, Dad, let's lower the volume just a smidge, okay?" and treat him with kid gloves, always trying to smooth things over. She'll fluff his pillows and ask if he needs anything else just to keep him happy. But me? I just don't have the patience or the bandwidth for that kind of diplomatic tap dance anymore. 

I mean, I'm not screaming at the guy. I know he's older, I know his health isn't great, and I'm not going out of my way to pick fights with him. But I'm absolutely not tiptoeing around trying to dodge an argument, either. If he does something that crosses a line or drives me crazy, I'll call it out. If a conflict happens, it happens. We bump heads, I say my piece, and I move on. So, yeah, no special tactics from me to avoid arguing. I just tell it like it is.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience a full range of emotions when you're at home with your father-in-law?

Unable to feel things? No, no way. It's honestly the exact opposite. If anything, I am feeling way too many emotions all at once, and I'd love to just dial them back a bit. 

You know, in EMS, you see guys who have been riding the rig for twenty, thirty years, and they get that... that numbness. They just stop feeling things. You could have the most chaotic, heartbreaking call—a bad pediatric trauma or something—and they just pack up the bags, wash out the back of the ambulance, and go eat a sandwich like nothing happened. They've totally walled off their emotions just to survive the job. I've always been really careful not to let myself get like that. I've always made sure I process what I see. But right now, at home? With him there? The walls are completely down. 

I am feeling the entire spectrum, doc, loud and clear. I walk in the door and I instantly feel this spike of irritation because it's 78 degrees and stuffy. Then he does that tongue-clicking thing, and I feel genuine, boiling anger—which is ridiculous, I know, it's just a noise, but it makes my blood pressure shoot up. And then, almost immediately, I feel this heavy, sinking guilt. Because I look at him, and I see a sick older guy who can't live on his own anymore, surrounded by pill bottles and oxygen tubing, and I feel pity. I feel bad for him. And I feel terrible for being so angry at him when he's just existing in my house. 

Then my wife walks in, and I feel this deep ache for her, because I see how stressed she is trying to manage him and manage me, and I just feel completely helpless. So I'm bouncing from irritated, to resentful, to guilty, to sad, to just plain exhausted, all in the span of like, an hour. It's a total rollercoaster. So, no, I'm definitely not blocked off or unable to feel things. I'm feeling every single bit of it, every day, and honestly... it's exhausting. It takes so much energy to feel this much all the time in your own living room.
Do you ever feel like you're observing yourself from outside your body when you're at home with your father-in-law?

Outside my body? Like... floating above the room, looking down at myself? No. No, definitely not. I mean, I've heard of that happening to people. You know, in my line of work, you get patients who have been through a massive trauma, maybe a bad rollover on the interstate, and they're in shock. They'll tell you later that they felt like they were watching us cut them out of the car from up on the highway overpass or something. It’s a real thing that the brain does to protect itself, I completely get that. But me? No, I am very, very much stuck inside my own body. 

Honestly, there are days I kind of wish I could just float away for a minute, just to get a break from it all. But no, I am hyper-aware of my physical self when I'm in that house. I can feel the sweat on the back of my neck because, like I said, he keeps it at 78 degrees in there all the time. I can feel the tension in my jaw, I can feel the exact moment a headache starts right behind my eyes when that TV gets turned up to maximum volume for the evening news. I'm just a tired, 51-year-old guy sitting on a couch that smells like menthol rub, feeling every single ache in my lower back from lifting stretchers and carrying gear all night. 

There's no detachment at all. I am entirely in my own skin, feeling every uncomfortable minute of it. It's just... it's a very grounded, very physical exhaustion. I'm right there on the couch, very aware that I'm the one sitting there. So, no, I've never had that out-of-body feeling, not at work, and definitely not sitting in my own living room.
Do you ever feel like things around you at home are unreal or distant when your father-in-law is there?

Unreal? No, no, definitely not. It’s actually funny you ask that, because honestly, it’s the exact opposite. Everything is painfully real. It's so real it's almost suffocating, if I'm being completely honest with you. 

Like... I know what you mean by that. I do. We get calls sometimes where a patient is in acute shock, maybe they've lost a lot of blood or they've just witnessed something horrific, and they'll look around with this blank stare and say, "This feels like a dream," or "Am I in a movie?" Their brain just sort of disconnects from the environment to protect them from the trauma of it all. I completely get the physiology of it, I've seen it a hundred times. But for me? When I'm at home? No. There is absolutely zero distance between me and what's going on in that house. 

I don't feel like I'm in a fog or looking through a dirty window or anything like that. I see every single detail, probably way more than I even want to. I see the exact way his slippers are kicked off right in the middle of the hallway where someone could trip over them in the dark. I see the condensation dripping down his glass of ice water that he leaves right on the good wood end table without a coaster—which, you know, my wife absolutely hates, it ruins the finish, but she won't say a single word to him about it because she doesn't want to rock the boat. 

And the sounds... there's nothing distant about the sounds. Like I said about the TV, I hear every single commercial. Have you ever noticed how much louder car commercials are than the actual news broadcast? Because I have. I know every jingle for every local car dealership by heart now because it just echoes through the drywall straight into the kitchen. I hear the exact rhythm of his breathing, I hear the ice clinking in his glass, I hear the floorboards creak when he shifts his weight in his recliner. 

So, no, there's no feeling of things being distant or fake or unreal. I'm sitting there, smelling that medicinal, menthol smell he brings with him everywhere, feeling the heat radiating because the thermostat is cranked up, and it is one hundred percent, undeniable reality. Sometimes I think it would be nice if things got a little fuzzy or distant, just to give my brain a break from the constant sensory input, you know? Just a five-minute mental vacation where the room goes out of focus. But no, my brain doesn't do that. I am completely, stubbornly anchored to the room, taking in every single sight and sound, and it just... it never stops. It's all very, very real.
Do you feel like you're unable to feel positive emotions, such as happiness or excitement, when you're at home with your father-in-law?

Unable to feel positive emotions? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's not like I'm walking around under a black cloud where I can't smile or enjoy things. I definitely still feel happiness and excitement. 

Like, when my daughter calls from college to tell us about her classes, I still feel that huge rush of pride and joy. My wife and I will be on speakerphone with her, laughing and just feeling really good about how well she's doing. Even with him sitting right there in the living room, doing his crossword puzzle or whatever, I'm still completely capable of feeling happy in that moment. Or, you know, just the small things. When I get off a really brutal night shift and I finally sit down with a hot cup of coffee on the back porch before the rest of the neighborhood wakes up... I feel genuinely content. I love that quiet time. I still really enjoy a good meal, or watching a football game if I can actually hear the announcers over his shows. So the capacity for joy is absolutely still there. I'm not numb to the good stuff. 

It's just that... well, it feels like those positive moments are a lot more fragile now, if that makes sense. Like, my wife and I will be in the kitchen, having a great conversation, maybe laughing about some ridiculous thing one of the rookies did at the station—because I swear, the new kids they hire, they have zero common sense, they just memorize the protocol book and freeze up when a patient actually talks to them—so we'll be laughing about that, feeling genuinely happy and connected. And then, right in the middle of it, he’ll yell from the other room that his soup is too cold or that he dropped the remote, and... bam. The moment is just gone. The happiness just evaporates and gets instantly replaced by that irritation I was talking about earlier. 

But the ability to feel the happiness in the first place? No, I haven't lost that at all. It just gets interrupted a lot. I just wish I could hold onto those good feelings a little longer before the reality of the house crashes back in, you know?
Do you ever feel like you're not yourself when you're at home with your father-in-law?

Not myself? Hmm. No, I wouldn't say that. I'm definitely still me. I mean, I'm a fifty-one-year-old guy who's been doing the same job for a long time, I know exactly who I am and how I like to live. If anything, the problem is that I am very much myself, and my usual way of living is just completely clashing with him being in the house. 

Like, I'm still the exact same guy who needs a solid thirty minutes of absolute quiet after a shift. You know, you spend twelve hours in the back of an ambulance with sirens blaring, dispatch radios squawking, people sometimes literally screaming at you... when I walk through my front door, I just want to drop my boots in the mudroom, put my keys in the little wooden bowl on the console table, and just sit and breathe. That's who I am. That's who I've always been. 

And I'm still that guy. It's just that now, when I go to put my keys in the bowl, his spare reading glasses and his Tuesday-Thursday pill organizers are already sitting in it. And when I want that thirty minutes of quiet, I'm instead listening to him argue out loud with the contestants on Jeopardy. 

So, no, my personality hasn't changed. I don't feel like a stranger in my own head or anything weird like that. I don't feel like I've lost my identity. I'm the exact same me, just... maybe a highly irritable version of me who has to bite his tongue so hard it almost bleeds just to keep the peace for my wife's sake. But the core of who I am? My thoughts, my reactions, my preferences? That's all still one hundred percent me. I haven't turned into somebody else. I just have a lot less room to actually *be* myself right now, if that makes sense. But I'm definitely still in here.
Do you feel like you've become less responsive to things that normally would upset or bother you since your father-in-law moved in?

Less responsive? Like, numb? No, definitely not. Honestly, if anything, I’m probably *more* responsive to things that bother me right now, just because my baseline stress level is sitting so much higher than it usually does. 

Like, take work, for example. In my line of work, you deal with upsetting things all day long. You have to have a thick skin, or you'd never survive a week on the trucks. But you still get annoyed by the day-to-day stuff, right? Like people who don't pull over for the sirens. I swear, nobody looks in their rearview mirrors anymore. They're texting, or they've got their music cranked up, or they're just completely oblivious to a massive flashing ambulance right on their bumper. Usually, I just hit the air horn, shake my head, and safely maneuver around them. It’s annoying, but it’s just part of the job. I've been doing it for decades, I'm used to it.

But lately? Since he moved in? When someone doesn't yield, I can physically feel my jaw clenching. I'm gripping the steering wheel so tight my knuckles are white, and I'm just fuming. It bothers me way more than it used to. And it's the same thing with those rookies at the station I was telling you about. Usually, I have a lot of patience for the new guys. We all had to start somewhere, and I don't mind walking them through how to properly restock the jump bag or clean the back of the rig. But the other day, one of them left the spare oxygen tanks unsecured, and I just snapped at him. I didn't scream or anything, but I was definitely a lot sharper than I normally would be. 

And it's the little stuff outside of work, too. If the grocery store is out of my usual brand of coffee, or if the guy in front of me at the checkout is taking forever to count out exact change... normally I’d just sigh and wait it out. Now? It feels like this huge, monumental inconvenience. I can feel myself getting hot under the collar over things that really shouldn't matter. It's because I’m already so drained from the second I wake up, knowing I have to navigate around his slippers and listen to him complain about the morning news anchors. 

So no, I haven't stopped reacting to things that upset me. I haven't shut down or gotten numb to the world. I feel like every single minor annoyance is just magnified right now because my patience is completely tapped out. I just don't have the bandwidth to brush things off the way I used to.
Are you avoiding social interactions or activities outside of home because of your father-in-law's presence?

Avoiding? Well, it's not like I'm hiding in my bedroom refusing to go out in public, if that's what you mean. I'm still going to work, obviously. I'm still doing my regular EMT shifts, pulling my weight on the trucks, because, you know, we have a mortgage and now we have an extra mouth to feed and higher utility bills with him being in the house all day with the heat cranked up to eighty. So the day-to-day job is absolutely still happening. I haven't missed a shift. 

But as far as other stuff outside the house? Yeah, I guess I have been pulling back a lot. 

Like, for the last year or so, I’ve been chipping away at my paramedic coursework. It’s a pretty big step up from basic EMT, lots of heavy studying—pharmacology, cardiology, advanced airway management, all that stuff. I used to come home, get that thirty minutes of quiet I talked about, make a pot of coffee, and then knock out a module or two on my laptop at the kitchen island. But lately? I’ve completely fallen behind. I try to open the laptop, and he's right there at the table asking me how to fix the volume on his iPad, or complaining that the Wi-Fi is too slow for his Facebook videos, and I just... I can't concentrate. The peace and quiet I need to actually absorb the material just doesn't exist anymore. So I just close the laptop. I honestly haven't logged into the portal for weeks, and my instructor is starting to send me reminder emails that I'm just ignoring. 

And then there's the community first-aid workshops. For years, I’ve been volunteering on my off days to help run these free clinics at the local rec center or the high schools. We teach CPR to new parents, show local coaches how to pack a wound or use an AED, that kind of thing. It used to be something I really looked forward to. It's a great group of guys from the station, and we usually go grab a beer and a burger afterwards. It was a nice social thing. But recently, I’ve just stopped showing up consistently. 

The guy who coordinates it, Dave, he texted me last week asking if I was gonna make the Saturday morning session, and I just made up some excuse about picking up an extra shift. The truth is, by the time my weekend rolls around, I am just so mentally exhausted from navigating the minefield of my own living room that the idea of standing in a gymnasium for three hours, being peppy and social and answering questions from strangers... I just don't have it in me. My social battery is completely drained by the time I walk out my front door. So I just end up staying home, which is ironic because home is the exact place that's stressing me out, but I just don't have the energy to go out and do the extra stuff I used to enjoy.
Do you feel like you've become less sensitive to emotional stimuli since your father-in-law moved in?

Less sensitive? No, I think... I mean, that's kind of like what you asked a minute ago about being numb, right? But if you mean emotional stuff specifically, like feeling sad or empathetic or just, you know, being moved by things... no, definitely not. Honestly, it's the exact opposite. I feel like an absolute raw nerve lately. 

In my line of work, you see a lot of heavy, heavy stuff. You'd think after twenty-plus years on an ambulance, I'd be completely emotionally blunted by now, but I'm really not. When we get a call for a sick kid, or an elderly person who fell and their spouse of fifty years is standing there crying in the hallway... that still gets to me. It always has. target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depersonalization (feeling like observing oneself from outside the body), which is not part of my symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder.

patient.answer:
Outside my body? Like... floating above the room, looking down at myself? No. No, definitely not. I mean, I've heard of that happening to people. You know, in my line of work, you get patients who have been through a massive trauma, maybe a bad rollover on the interstate, and they're in shock. They'll tell you later that they felt like they were watching us cut them out of the car from up on the highway overpass or something. It’s a real thing that the brain does to protect itself, I completely get that. But me? No, I am very, very much stuck inside my own body. 

Honestly, there are days I kind of wish I could just float away for a minute, just to get a break from it all. But no, I am hyper-aware of my physical self when I'm in that house. I can feel the sweat on the back of my neck because, like I said, he keeps it at 78 degrees in there all the time. I can feel the tension in my jaw, I can feel the exact moment a headache starts right behind my eyes when that TV gets turned up to maximum volume for the evening news. I'm just a tired, 51-year-old guy sitting on a couch that smells like menthol rub, feeling every single ache in my lower back from lifting stretchers and carrying gear all night. 

There's no detachment at all. I am entirely in my own skin, feeling every uncomfortable minute of it. It's just... it's a very grounded, very physical exhaustion. I'm right there on the couch, very aware that I'm the one sitting there. So, no, I've never had that out-of-body feeling, not at work, and definitely not sitting in my own living room.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient is experiencing derealization
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like things around you at home are unreal or distant when your father-in-law is there?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of derealization (feeling that surroundings are unreal or distant), which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Unreal? No, no, definitely not. It’s actually funny you ask that, because honestly, it’s the exact opposite. Everything is painfully real. It's so real it's almost suffocating, if I'm being completely honest with you. 

Like... I know what you mean by that. I do. We get calls sometimes where a patient is in acute shock, maybe they've lost a lot of blood or they've just witnessed something horrific, and they'll look around with this blank stare and say, "This feels like a dream," or "Am I in a movie?" Their brain just sort of disconnects from the environment to protect them from the trauma of it all. I completely get the physiology of it, I've seen it a hundred times. But for me? When I'm at home? No. There is absolutely zero distance between me and what's going on in that house. 

I don't feel like I'm in a fog or looking through a dirty window or anything like that. I see every single detail, probably way more than I even want to. I see the exact way his slippers are kicked off right in the middle of the hallway where someone could trip over them in the dark. I see the condensation dripping down his glass of ice water that he leaves right on the good wood end table without a coaster—which, you know, my wife absolutely hates, it ruins the finish, but she won't say a single word to him about it because she doesn't want to rock the boat. 

And the sounds... there's nothing distant about the sounds. Like I said about the TV, I hear every single commercial. Have you ever noticed how much louder car commercials are than the actual news broadcast? Because I have. I know every jingle for every local car dealership by heart now because it just echoes through the drywall straight into the kitchen. I hear the exact rhythm of his breathing, I hear the ice clinking in his glass, I hear the floorboards creak when he shifts his weight in his recliner. 

So, no, there's no feeling of things being distant or fake or unreal. I'm sitting there, smelling that medicinal, menthol smell he brings with him everywhere, feeling the heat radiating because the thermostat is cranked up, and it is one hundred percent, undeniable reality. Sometimes I think it would be nice if things got a little fuzzy or distant, just to give my brain a break from the constant sensory input, you know? Just a five-minute mental vacation where the room goes out of focus. But no, my brain doesn't do that. I am completely, stubbornly anchored to the room, taking in every single sight and sound, and it just... it never stops. It's all very, very real.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient is experiencing emotional numbing
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're unable to feel positive emotions, such as happiness or excitement, when you're at home with your father-in-law?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the inability to experience positive emotions, which is a symptom of conditions like depression or PTSD, but this is not included in my symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder.

patient.answer:
Unable to feel positive emotions? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's not like I'm walking around under a black cloud where I can't smile or enjoy things. I definitely still feel happiness and excitement. 

Like, when my daughter calls from college to tell us about her classes, I still feel that huge rush of pride and joy. My wife and I will be on speakerphone with her, laughing and just feeling really good about how well she's doing. Even with him sitting right there in the living room, doing his crossword puzzle or whatever, I'm still completely capable of feeling happy in that moment. Or, you know, just the small things. When I get off a really brutal night shift and I finally sit down with a hot cup of coffee on the back porch before the rest of the neighborhood wakes up... I feel genuinely content. I love that quiet time. I still really enjoy a good meal, or watching a football game if I can actually hear the announcers over his shows. So the capacity for joy is absolutely still there. I'm not numb to the good stuff. 

It's just that... well, it feels like those positive moments are a lot more fragile now, if that makes sense. Like, my wife and I will be in the kitchen, having a great conversation, maybe laughing about some ridiculous thing one of the rookies did at the station—because I swear, the new kids they hire, they have zero common sense, they just memorize the protocol book and freeze up when a patient actually talks to them—so we'll be laughing about that, feeling genuinely happy and connected. And then, right in the middle of it, he’ll yell from the other room that his soup is too cold or that he dropped the remote, and... bam. The moment is just gone. The happiness just evaporates and gets instantly replaced by that irritation I was talking about earlier. 

But the ability to feel the happiness in the first place? No, I haven't lost that at all. It just gets interrupted a lot. I just wish I could hold onto those good feelings a little longer before the reality of the house crashes back in, you know?

doctor.intent: determine if the patient is experiencing dissociative symptoms
doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you're not yourself when you're at home with your father-in-law?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depersonalization or an altered sense of identity/self, which is a dissociative symptom. This is not covered by my symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder.

patient.answer:
Not myself? Hmm. No, I wouldn't say that. I'm definitely still me. I mean, I'm a fifty-one-year-old guy who's been doing the same job for a long time, I know exactly who I am and how I like to live. If anything, the problem is that I am very much myself, and my usual way of living is just completely clashing with him being in the house. 

Like, I'm still the exact same guy who needs a solid thirty minutes of absolute quiet after a shift. You know, you spend twelve hours in the back of an ambulance with sirens blaring, dispatch radios squawking, people sometimes literally screaming at you... when I walk through my front door, I just want to drop my boots in the mudroom, put my keys in the little wooden bowl on the console table, and just sit and breathe. That's who I am. That's who I've always been. 

And I'm still that guy. It's just that now, when I go to put my keys in the bowl, his spare reading glasses and his Tuesday-Thursday pill organizers are already sitting in it. And when I want that thirty minutes of quiet, I'm instead listening to him argue out loud with the contestants on Jeopardy. 

So, no, my personality hasn't changed. I don't feel like a stranger in my own head or anything weird like that. I don't feel like I've lost my identity. I'm the exact same me, just... maybe a highly irritable version of me who has to bite his tongue so hard it almost bleeds just to keep the peace for my wife's sake. But the core of who I am? My thoughts, my reactions, my preferences? That's all still one hundred percent me. I haven't turned into somebody else. I just have a lot less room to actually *be* myself right now, if that makes sense. But I'm definitely still in here.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient is experiencing emotional numbing
doctor.question: Do you feel like you've become less responsive to things that normally would upset or bother you since your father-in-law moved in?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotional numbing or reduced responsiveness, which is not covered by the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Less responsive? Like, numb? No, definitely not. Honestly, if anything, I’m probably *more* responsive to things that bother me right now, just because my baseline stress level is sitting so much higher than it usually does. 

Like, take work, for example. In my line of work, you deal with upsetting things all day long. You have to have a thick skin, or you'd never survive a week on the trucks. But you still get annoyed by the day-to-day stuff, right? Like people who don't pull over for the sirens. I swear, nobody looks in their rearview mirrors anymore. They're texting, or they've got their music cranked up, or they're just completely oblivious to a massive flashing ambulance right on their bumper. Usually, I just hit the air horn, shake my head, and safely maneuver around them. It’s annoying, but it’s just part of the job. I've been doing it for decades, I'm used to it.

But lately? Since he moved in? When someone doesn't yield, I can physically feel my jaw clenching. I'm gripping the steering wheel so tight my knuckles are white, and I'm just fuming. It bothers me way more than it used to. And it's the same thing with those rookies at the station I was telling you about. Usually, I have a lot of patience for the new guys. We all had to start somewhere, and I don't mind walking them through how to properly restock the jump bag or clean the back of the rig. But the other day, one of them left the spare oxygen tanks unsecured, and I just snapped at him. I didn't scream or anything, but I was definitely a lot sharper than I normally would be. 

And it's the little stuff outside of work, too. If the grocery store is out of my usual brand of coffee, or if the guy in front of me at the checkout is taking forever to count out exact change... normally I’d just sigh and wait it out. Now? It feels like this huge, monumental inconvenience. I can feel myself getting hot under the collar over things that really shouldn't matter. It's because I’m already so drained from the second I wake up, knowing I have to navigate around his slippers and listen to him complain about the morning news anchors. 

So no, I haven't stopped reacting to things that upset me. I haven't shut down or gotten numb to the world. I feel like every single minor annoyance is just magnified right now because my patience is completely tapped out. I just don't have the bandwidth to brush things off the way I used to.

patient.answer:
Avoiding? Well, it's not like I'm hiding in my bedroom refusing to go out in public, if that's what you mean. I'm still going to work, obviously. I'm still doing my regular EMT shifts, pulling my weight on the trucks, because, you know, we have a mortgage and now we have an extra mouth to feed and higher utility bills with him being in the house all day with the heat cranked up to eighty. So the day-to-day job is absolutely still happening. I haven't missed a shift. 

But as far as other stuff outside the house? Yeah, I guess I have been pulling back a lot. 

Like, for the last year or so, I’ve been chipping away at my paramedic coursework. It’s a pretty big step up from basic EMT, lots of heavy studying—pharmacology, cardiology, advanced airway management, all that stuff. I used to come home, get that thirty minutes of quiet I talked about, make a pot of coffee, and then knock out a module or two on my laptop at the kitchen island. But lately? I’ve completely fallen behind. I try to open the laptop, and he's right there at the table asking me how to fix the volume on his iPad, or complaining that the Wi-Fi is too slow for his Facebook videos, and I just... I can't concentrate. The peace and quiet I need to actually absorb the material just doesn't exist anymore. So I just close the laptop. I honestly haven't logged into the portal for weeks, and my instructor is starting to send me reminder emails that I'm just ignoring. 

And then there's the community first-aid workshops. For years, I’ve been volunteering on my off days to help run these free clinics at the local rec center or the high schools. We teach CPR to new parents, show local coaches how to pack a wound or use an AED, that kind of thing. It used to be something I really looked forward to. It's a great group of guys from the station, and we usually go grab a beer and a burger afterwards. It was a nice social thing. But recently, I’ve just stopped showing up consistently. 

The guy who coordinates it, Dave, he texted me last week asking if I was gonna make the Saturday morning session, and I just made up some excuse about picking up an extra shift. The truth is, by the time my weekend rolls around, I am just so mentally exhausted from navigating the minefield of my own living room that the idea of standing in a gymnasium for three hours, being peppy and social and answering questions from strangers... I just don't have it in me. My social battery is completely drained by the time I walk out my front door. So I just end up staying home, which is ironic because home is the exact place that's stressing me out, but I just don't have the energy to go out and do the extra stuff I used to enjoy.

patient.answer:
Less sensitive? No, I think... I mean, that's kind of like what you asked a minute ago about being numb, right? But if you mean emotional stuff specifically, like feeling sad or empathetic or just, you know, being moved by things... no, definitely not. Honestly, it's the exact opposite. I feel like an absolute raw nerve lately. 

In my line of work, you see a lot of heavy, heavy stuff. You'd think after twenty-plus years on an ambulance, I'd be completely emotionally blunted by now, but I'm really not. When we get a call for a sick kid, or an elderly person who fell and their spouse of fifty years is standing there crying in the hallway... that still gets to me. It always has. But since my father-in-law moved in? Man, my emotions are just right there at the surface all the time. 

Like, the other night, my wife was watching one of those cheesy Hallmark movies in the living room. I usually just tune them out—you know the ones, where the big city lawyer goes back to her hometown to save a bakery or whatever. I was just sitting there on the couch, trying to ignore her dad complaining about the volume, and I actually felt myself tearing up a little bit. Over a Hallmark movie! And it wasn't even a sad part, it was just... the house in the movie looked so peaceful, and the people were just talking to each other normally without any tension, and it just hit me how much I miss that feeling in my own home. It's ridiculous, I know. A fifty-one-year-old guy getting choked up over a cable TV movie. 

So no, I haven't lost my sensitivity. It's like my emotional skin has just been peeled back. Every little thing, whether it's sad, or frustrating, or even just mildly touching, it hits me way harder than it normally would. I see these families on the job dealing with a crisis, and I'm feeling so bad for them because I know how hard family dynamics can be even *without* a medical emergency thrown in. And at home, I'm hypersensitive to my wife's moods, too. I can tell when she's feeling guilty about the strain her dad is putting on us, and that makes me feel incredibly guilty for being so annoyed all the time, and then it's just this whole big emotional feedback loop that goes round and round. 

If there was a switch to turn down my sensitivity right now, I'd probably flip it just to get a break, to be completely honest with you. Because feeling everything at a ten out of ten all day long, carrying all that emotional weight at work and then carrying a whole different set of emotional baggage at home... it's exhausting. But no, the sensitivity is very, very much still there. I haven't shut down emotionally at all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient is experiencing emotional numbing
doctor.question: Do you feel like you've become less reactive to things that would normally upset or disturb you since your father-in-law moved in?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about emotional numbing or decreased emotional reactivity, which is not part of my Adjustment Disorder symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Less reactive? No, no, I think... well, I know we kind of just touched on this a few minutes ago when you asked about me being less sensitive, but it really is the exact opposite. If anything, I'm reacting way *more* to things that used to just roll right off my back. 

I mean, take my job, for instance. On the ambulance, you see disturbing things all the time. A bad traffic collision on the interstate, or someone who's had a really severe medical episode, lots of blood, whatever it might be. For years, I could just completely compartmentalize that. I’d run through the protocols, get the patient to the ER, hand off the chart, and then my partner and I would go grab a coffee and I wouldn't think twice about it. It’s just the job. But lately? Man, I see something upsetting and it just sticks to me. It's like my defenses are completely down. 

Like, the other day we had a call for a guy who took a really bad fall down some concrete steps. Nasty head laceration, and he was really confused and scared. Normally, I'd just stay calm, grab the gauze, apply pressure, and keep him talking. And I did all that, but there were these bystanders just standing around filming it on their phones, and I found myself getting incredibly angry. Like, my blood was just boiling. I actually snapped at one of them, told them to have some respect and put the phone away, which is... I mean, it's true, but it's not really professional for me to lose my cool like that. I was just so deeply irritated by it. 

And it's not just the heavy stuff at work, it's the stuff at home, too. Normally, if my father-in-law made some passive-aggressive comment about dinner being too salty, or if he was watching those loud political shows and getting all worked up over the news, I would have just rolled my eyes and gone out to the garage to tinker with my tools or something. I would have just let it go. But now? Now I hear it and I get so instantly worked up. I have to physically bite my tongue so I don't just explode at him over something stupid like the volume of the TV or his complaints about the brand of orange juice my wife bought. And then I get mad at myself for getting mad, because I know it stresses my wife out when we argue. 

So, no, I definitely haven't become less reactive. Honestly, I wish I was! It would make getting through the day a whole lot easier if I could just let things go or tune out the disturbing stuff like I used to. But right now, every little annoyance or upsetting thing just hooks right into me, and I can't seem to shake it off.
